meanings.note: Used as a quick imperative olha! (look!) and in future subjunctive se vocês olharem (if you look).

examples.text: Se vocês olharem bem, tem números.
examples.trans: If you look closely, there are numbers.

meanings.note: Definite article agreeing in gender and number with its noun; also common before given names in casual Brazilian speech.

examples.trans: Look at the young woman over there.

meanings.note: Expresses duration (por uma hora) and fixed phrases like por exemplo.

examples.trans: I stayed there for an hour.

meanings.note: Used in por exemplo (for example) to point to a concrete case.
Informal reduced para. Before a feminine noun, this Brazilian spelling can also represent a contraction including the article a; the exact meeting is clear from context.

examples.trans: Are you going to the meeting?

meanings.note: Third-person feminine singular pronoun; in informal Brazilian speech olha pra ela uses ela after a preposition too.
All-purpose connector, relative link, question opener, and comparative word after mais or melhor.

examples.text: Eu acho que ele já foi.
examples.trans: I think that he already left.

meanings.note: Expresses possession, obligation in ter que + infinitive, and impersonal existence (tem alguns números, there are some numbers).

examples.text: Eu tenho que entrar lá dentro.
examples.trans: I have to go inside there.

meanings.note: Means failing to attend a class, shift, or meeting (faltou a uma reunião).
Links verbs like faltar to an event or destination.
Indefinite article; plural uns and umas mean some or a few in everyday Brazilian Portuguese.

examples.trans: Shall we have a little coffee?

meanings.note: A gathering of people for a purpose. Here a workplace meeting; the final diphthong is nasal.

examples.trans: I’m not going to the meeting.

meanings.note: Coordinating conjunction pronounced [i] in natural Brazilian speech.

examples.text: Ela faltou e adiantou o trabalho.
examples.trans: She missed it and got ahead on her work.
There are good and bad numbers.

meanings.note: From adiante (ahead): adiantar o trabalho means getting ahead on your tasks.

examples.trans: She got ahead on her work.
I'll get ahead on this part today.

meanings.note: Tasks to complete or one's employment.

examples.trans: She got ahead on her work.
I have a lot of work today.

meanings.note: Contraction of de + ela, placed after the noun in Brazil to mean her.

examples.trans: She got ahead on her work.

meanings.note: Limits a statement (eu só quero) or forms só que (except that / the catch is).

examples.text: Eu só quero saber o motivo.
examples.trans: I just want to know the reason.

examples.text: Só que agora ela precisa de ajuda.

meanings.note: Marks the current moment resulting from an earlier action.

examples.trans: Now she is in a meeting.

examples.text: Agora tenho que resolver umas coisinhas.
examples.trans: Right now I have to sort out a few little things.

meanings.note: Takes de before a noun (precisa da ajuda) and links directly to an infinitive (precisava gritar).

examples.text: Ela precisa da ajuda do colega.

examples.trans: Did you need to shout at me?

meanings.note: Links a meeting with its subject. Do is de + the masculine article o; sou do financeiro identifies membership in the finance department.
Support needed from a coworker, often in precisar da ajuda de alguém.

examples.text: Ela precisa da ajuda do colega.

meanings.note: Used here for being present at an event. Vou estar keeps estar in the infinitive after the finite form vou.

examples.trans: I’m not going to be at that meeting.
Are you going to be at that meeting?

meanings.note: Usually contracts with definite articles to no, na, nos, nas.
An English loan used for the business activity of marketing. This line shortens the original marketing-planning meeting to a marketing meeting.
A negative answer or a negation in a sentence. A final repeated não can reinforce a conversational refusal in Brazil.
Irregular past eu fiz (I made/did); não tem o que fazer means having nothing to do.

examples.text: Ela não tem o que fazer agora.
examples.trans: She has nothing to do now.

examples.text: Esse slide aqui eu fiz ontem.
examples.trans: This slide here I made yesterday.

meanings.note: Expresses staying in a place or state (ficar sentado, fica no celular).

examples.text: Ela fica no celular o dia todo.
examples.trans: She stays on her phone all day.

meanings.note: Standard Brazilian word for a mobile phone.

examples.trans: My phone is on the desk.

meanings.note: Used for identifying a type of meeting or the department a person belongs to. The present forms sou and é are irregular.
Neutral demonstrative pronoun pointing to what was just said or done.

A person being addressed, with third-person verb agreement: você vai, vocês vão. Vai and vão are forms of ir, not forms of the pronoun. Common in Brazil; not a rule that every Brazilian region uses the same address system.

examples.trans: Are you going to the meeting?

meanings.note: Followed by an infinitive for your own wish (quero saber) or que + subjunctive for someone else (quero que você entre).

examples.text: Eu só quero saber o motivo.
examples.trans: I just want to know the reason.

meanings.note: Possessive determiner agreeing with the possessed noun; in Brazil it most often means your (with você).

examples.text: É isso que você quer pra sua vida?
examples.trans: Is that what you want for your life?

meanings.note: One's life or daily existence.

examples.text: É isso que você quer pra sua vida?
examples.trans: Is that what you want for your life?

examples.text: A vida no escritório é corrida.

meanings.note: Used for losing focus, wasting time, or missing transport.

examples.trans: I don't want to lose focus.
We lost a lot of time today.

meanings.note: Concentration on work; perder o foco means to lose focus.

examples.trans: I don't want to lose focus.

meanings.note: Subject form referring to the speaker. Explicit eu introduces his department in the explanation.
With que it is Brazil's most natural everyday way to say I think / do you think.

examples.text: Eu acho que você tá exagerando.

meanings.note: Overstating a problem; gerund exagerando pairs with estar.

examples.text: Eu acho que você tá exagerando.

meanings.note: Construes with com in Portuguese (gritar comigo, shout at me).

examples.trans: Did you need to shout at me?

meanings.note: Special fused form of com + mim; Portuguese says gritar comigo where English says shout at me.

examples.trans: Did you need to shout at me?
Come to the meeting with me.

meanings.note: Used in na frente de (in front of someone).

examples.text: Não grita na frente dos outros!
examples.trans: Don't shout in front of everyone else!

examples.text: Te espero na frente da sala.
examples.trans: I'll wait for you in front of the room.

meanings.note: Stands without um for another (outro gráfico), or with os for the others (os outros).
Open-handed or magnanimous; opens vowel to [ɔ] in feminine and plural forms.
Warm address among colleagues or ironical buddy in an argument.

examples.text: Ele é meu amigo do trabalho.
examples.trans: He is my friend from work.

meanings.note: Everyday friendly farewell across Brazil, borrowed long ago from Italian ciao.
